title: Numbers, division and slicing
summary: How division and remainders behave, why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and how to cut out part of a list or string.

sections.heading: Division
body: Dividing with `/` can give a decimal. For a whole-number result use `Math.floor` in JavaScript or `//` in Python. `%` gives the remainder.
Both "floor" towards minus infinity, so `-7 / 2` floored is `-4`, not `-3`. In Python, `/` always gives a float, even for `6 / 2`.

sections.heading: Decimals are not exact
body: Computers store decimals in binary, so some, like 0.1, are slightly off. Round when you display them, and never compare decimals with `===` or `==`.

sections.heading: Slicing: cut out a piece
body: A slice takes a start index and an end index. The start is included and the end is not, so `slice(1, 3)` gives items 1 and 2. Negative numbers count from the end.
Python slices can also take a step: `[::-1]` walks backwards and reverses.

javascript.code:
const letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']
console.log(letters.slice(1, 3))
console.log(letters.slice(-2))
console.log(letters.at(-1))
console.log('hello'.slice(1, 4))

mistakes: Expecting the end index of a slice to be included.
Writing `arr[-1]` in JavaScript: it is `undefined`. Use `arr.at(-1)`.
Using `/` in Python where you wanted a whole number (`//`).
